items.prompt: Sort the phrases into formal and informal.
hints: Think about where you would see each phrase: a letter to a stranger or a message to a friend.
Formal phrases are polite and complete. Informal ones are chatty.
Start with Hi there! Would you write that to a head teacher?
items.explanation: Dear Sir or Madam, Yours faithfully and I would be grateful if are formal. Hi there, See you soon and Thanks a lot are informal.

items.prompt: Which sentence is the most formal?

options.text: Can you tell us more about the trip?
options.why: This is polite but quite chatty.

options.text: Tell us more about the trip, please!
options.why: This is a friendly command, not formal.

options.text: What’s the deal with the trip?
options.why: This is slang.

options.text: We would like to request more information about the trip.

hints: Formal language is careful and polite.
Look for full words and more formal verbs.
Cross out anything with slang or contractions.
items.explanation: We would like to request uses full, polite words and a formal verb, request, instead of ask.

items.prompt: Match each informal phrase to a more formal word with the same meaning.
hints: Each pair means the same, but one is more formal.
Formal verbs are often single words that replace phrasal verbs like find out.
Start with ask for. Which formal verb is often used in letters?
items.explanation: Discover, request, receive, postpone, assist and require are more formal ways to say find out, ask for, get, put off, help and need.

items.prompt: Which ending suits a formal letter that began Dear Sir or Madam?

options.text: Yours sincerely,
options.why: Use Yours sincerely when you know the person’s name, as in Dear Mrs Lim.

options.text: Yours faithfully,
Love from,
options.why: This is for family and close friends.

options.text: Cheers,
options.why: This is very informal.

hints: Dear Sir or Madam means you do not know the person’s name.
British letters use different sign-offs for known and unknown names.
Cross out the informal sign-offs first, then decide between the two formal ones.
items.explanation: In British English, a letter that begins Dear Sir or Madam ends with Yours faithfully. A letter to a named person ends with Yours sincerely.

items.prompt: Write the contraction in full for a formal letter. We can’t attend the meeting.
hints: Contractions such as can’t are informal.
Write the full form of can’t.
In full, it is written as one word, not two.
items.explanation: Can’t is short for cannot, which is written as one word. Formal writing usually avoids contractions.

items.prompt: Choose all the features of informal writing.

options.text: contractions such as don’t
the passive voice, such as it was decided
options.why: The passive voice is common in formal writing.

options.text: exclamation marks for fun
full forms such as do not
options.why: Full forms are a feature of formal writing.

options.text: chatty phrases such as guess what

hints: Think about a message to a close friend.
Informal writing sounds like everyday speech.
Check each feature: would it appear in a text message to a friend?
items.explanation: Contractions, exclamation marks and chatty phrases make writing informal. The passive voice and full forms are more formal.

items.prompt: Which formal verb could replace look into? We need to look into the problem.

options.text: investigate
see
options.why: See is plain and does not mean the same as look into.

options.text: check out
options.why: Check out is another informal phrasal verb.

options.text: find
options.why: Find changes the meaning.

hints: Look into is a phrasal verb, which is often informal.
You need one formal verb that means examine carefully.
Try each option in the sentence: We need to ___ the problem.
items.explanation: Investigate means examine something carefully to find out the facts. It is the formal word for look into.

items.prompt: Which sentence is the best way to complain politely in a formal email to a shop?

options.text: Your bike is rubbish and the bell’s broken!
options.why: This is rude and informal.

options.text: Hey, the bell on my bike doesn’t work, sort it out.
options.why: Hey and sort it out are too informal and rude.

options.text: I am writing to inform you that the bicycle I purchased on 5 May arrived with a broken bell.
I’m really, really cross about my bike.
options.why: This shows feelings but does not explain the problem.

hints: A formal complaint is polite and clear.
It explains the facts: what you bought, when, and what is wrong.
Cross out any option with slang or rude words.
items.explanation: The correct sentence uses formal words such as inform and purchased and states the facts clearly and politely.

items.prompt: Which word in this formal sentence is too informal? We were delighted to receive loads of donations for the library appeal.

options.text: delighted
options.why: Delighted is a polite, formal way to show pleasure.

options.text: receive
options.why: Receive is a formal verb.

options.text: loads
donations
options.why: Donations is a formal word.

hints: Most of the sentence is formal. One word is chatty.
Imagine the sentence in a letter from a head teacher.
Which word would you replace with many or a large number of?
items.explanation: Loads is informal. A formal sentence would say many donations or a large number of donations.

items.prompt: Which is the best formal version of this message? Sorry, but the trip’s off cos of the rain.

options.text: Unfortunately, the trip has been cancelled because of the weather.
Sorry, the trip’s been cancelled cos it rained.
options.why: Cos and trip’s are still informal.

options.text: Unfortunately, the trip is off because of the rain, sorry!
options.why: Is off and sorry! keep it informal.

options.text: The trip has been cancelled, which is a real shame, guys.
options.why: Guys is informal.

hints: Look for informal words such as cos, off and sorry.
A formal version uses full forms and formal words, and often the passive voice.
Find the version with no contractions or slang at all.
items.explanation: Unfortunately is a formal way to say sorry, has been cancelled replaces is off and because of replaces cos of.

items.prompt: Which message would you send to a close friend?

options.text: I would be most grateful if you could confirm your attendance.
options.why: This is very formal for a friend.

options.text: Hey! Are you coming to my party on Saturday?
Dear Sir, I am writing to invite you to an event.
options.why: This sounds like a letter to a stranger or an official.

options.text: Your presence is requested at a social gathering.
options.why: This is formal and stiff for a friend.

hints: A friend is someone you know well.
Informal writing is relaxed and friendly.
Which sentence sounds like a message you would send quickly?
items.explanation: With a close friend you can use a friendly, relaxed tone. The other sentences are too formal.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences by where you would use them.
hints: Formal writing is polite and complete.
Informal writing can be short and use slang.
Start with Yours sincerely. Who would you write that to?
items.explanation: Short, relaxed phrases and slang are for friends. Polite, complete phrases and sign-offs suit a headteacher.

items.prompt: Dear Mrs Putri, I am writing to ask about the school trip. Yours ___. Dear Sir or Madam, I wish to complain. Yours ___.
hints: The ending depends on how the letter begins.
A named person goes with one ending and Sir or Madam goes with another.
Think about whether the writer knows the name of the reader.
items.explanation: Use Yours sincerely when you know the name. Use Yours faithfully after Dear Sir or Madam.

items.prompt: Match each informal word to a more formal word.
hints: Formal words are often longer and more exact.
Think of a word you would see in an official letter.
Start with sorry. What verb means to say sorry formally?
items.explanation: Each formal word has the same meaning as its informal partner but sounds more polite and serious.

items.prompt: Build a polite formal request. Use the cards.
items.answer: I would be grateful for your help.
hints: Formal writing avoids slang words like gonna.
Start with I.
The phrase would be grateful is polite.
items.explanation: I would be grateful for your help is a polite, formal way to ask. Gonna and wanna are informal.

items.prompt: Put the parts of a formal email in order.
items: Subject: Request to borrow the school hall
I am writing to ask whether our class may borrow the school hall.
We need it on Friday from 1 pm to 3 pm for a rehearsal.
I would be grateful if you could reply by Monday.
hints: A formal email starts with a subject line and a greeting.
State the purpose before the details.
The closing request comes just before the sign-off.
items.explanation: A formal email has a subject, a greeting, the purpose, the details, a polite closing request and a sign-off.

items.prompt: Which sentence is the best formal version of this message? Can you tell me when the bus leaves? Thanks!

options.text: Can u tell me when the bus goes? Thx.
options.why: Text-speak is not suitable for formal writing.

options.text: Tell me when the bus leaves.
options.why: This is too blunt and has no polite words.

options.text: Could you please inform me what time the bus departs? Thank you.
What time is the bus gonna leave?
options.why: Gonna is slang and the sentence is not polite enough.

hints: Formal writing is polite and complete.
Look for a polite question with careful words.
Avoid slang like gonna and shortened words like thx.
items.explanation: Could you please inform me and Thank you are polite and complete. The word departs is more formal than leaves.

items.prompt: Complete the table. Write formal or informal.
head: Feature
Which register?
hints: Informal writing sounds like talking.
Formal writing is careful and polite.
Slang and many exclamation marks are relaxed.
items.explanation: Contractions, slang and many exclamation marks make writing informal. Polite openings and full sentences are formal.

items.prompt: Write one formal word to replace kids. Parents should bring their kids to the meeting.
hints: Kids is an informal word.
A formal notice would use a more standard word.
What word do teachers use for young people at school?
items.explanation: Children is the standard formal word for kids.

items.prompt: Read this email. Which line is wrongly informal? (1) Dear Mr Hadi, (2) I am writing to ask about the school library. (3) Anyway, thanks a bunch, bye! (4) Yours sincerely, Wulan

options.text: line 1
options.why: Dear Mr Hadi is a correct formal greeting.

options.text: line 2
options.why: This is a formal opening that states the purpose.

options.text: line 3
line 4
options.why: Yours sincerely is a correct formal sign-off.

hints: Check each line for slang or casual words.
Match the tone of each line to a formal email.
Look for the line that sounds like a text to a friend.
items.explanation: Anyway, thanks a bunch and bye are casual. A formal email should end with a polite closing sentence instead.

items.prompt: Choose all the phrases suitable for a formal email to a museum.

options.text: I would like to enquire about school visits.
I look forward to hearing from you.
Thanks a million!
options.why: This is too chatty for a formal email.

options.text: Could you please confirm the opening times?
Hope you’re good!
options.why: This is a casual greeting for a friend.

hints: Formal phrases are polite and clear.
Casual greetings and slang do not belong in a formal email.
Check which phrases a teacher would be happy to see in an official letter.
items.explanation: Would like to enquire, could you please confirm and I look forward to hearing from you are polite and formal. The other two are casual.

items.prompt: Which notice gives the same information in a register suitable for a town council board?

options.text: Residents are advised that the car park will be closed on Saturday for repairs.
Heads up! The car park’s shut on Saturday coz of repairs.
options.why: Heads up and coz are informal.

options.text: Hey everyone, no parking Saturday, sorry!
options.why: This is friendly and chatty, not formal.

options.text: The car park is gonna be closed Saturday for fixing.
options.why: Gonna is slang.

hints: Think about who will read this notice.
Formal notices use careful words and passive phrases.
Residents are advised sounds official.
items.explanation: Formal notices use complete sentences, careful vocabulary and no slang. This one does that.

items.prompt: Maya is leaving a note for her classmate Leo about homework. Which note has the best register?

options.text: Dear Leo, I hereby inform you that the mathematics assignment is located on page 12.
options.why: This is far too formal for a note between classmates.

options.text: Leo, the maths homework is on page 12. See you tomorrow!
yo homework is p12 lol
options.why: This is too casual and unclear.

options.text: To whom it may concern, the homework is on page 12.
options.why: This is a formal opening and does not fit a note to a friend.

hints: The best register is not always the most formal one.
Think about who the reader is.
Pick the note that is friendly but still clear and complete.
items.explanation: A note between classmates should be friendly and clear. Very formal language would sound odd, and slang would be too casual and unclear.

items.prompt: Which email opening is both formal and clear about its purpose?

options.text: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing about the thing from last week.
options.why: It is formal but unclear, so the reader cannot tell the purpose.

options.text: Hi there, I want to know about swimming.
options.why: It is clear but too casual.

options.text: To the swimming person, please reply to me.
options.why: It is neither polite nor formal.

options.text: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to enquire about membership of your swimming club.

hints: A good formal opening has two jobs: be polite and say why you are writing.
Check each option for both jobs.
One option is formal but vague.
items.explanation: It uses a polite greeting and clearly states the purpose: to enquire about club membership.

items.prompt: You are writing a report on volcanoes. Which word names the molten rock that is still under the ground?

options.text: crater
options.why: A crater is the bowl-shaped opening at the top of a volcano.

options.text: ash
options.why: Ash is tiny pieces of rock thrown out by an eruption.

options.text: lava
options.why: Lava is molten rock after it has reached the surface.

options.text: magma

hints: Specialist words make a report accurate.
Think about where the rock is: under the ground or on top.
One word is used before an eruption, one after.
items.explanation: Magma is molten rock below the surface. Once it flows out of a volcano it is called lava.

items.prompt: Sort each topic word into the topic it belongs to.
hints: Think of a sentence for each word.
Orbit and galaxy are found far above the Earth.
Drizzle is a kind of light rain.
items.explanation: Specialist words belong to a topic: drizzle and humidity to weather, orbit and galaxy to space, tide and reef to the sea.

items.prompt: Water vapour cools and turns back into liquid water. This is called ___.
hints: The vapour is changing from gas to liquid.
Evaporation goes the other way.
Think of drops forming on a cold glass.
items.explanation: Condensation is the change of a gas into a liquid. Evaporation is the opposite change.

items.prompt: Match each specialist word to its meaning.
pairs: the place where an animal lives
an animal that eats only plants
hints: Each word belongs to the topic of animals.
Herbi is about plants. Noct is about night.
Start with predator and prey: who hunts whom?
items.explanation: These words help us write about animals accurately.

items.prompt: Which verb creates the strongest picture? The waves ___ against the cliffs in the storm.

options.text: touched
options.why: This is too gentle for a storm.

options.text: went
options.why: This is a weak, general verb.

options.text: hammered
were
options.why: This does not show any action.

hints: A storm is loud and strong.
Choose the verb that shows force.
Which verb could make the reader hear the sound?
items.explanation: Hammered gives a strong picture of waves hitting the cliffs hard. The other verbs are gentle or vague.

items.prompt: A thesaurus lists these words for walk: stroll, trudge, march, wander. Which fits a tired hiker at the end of a long day?

options.text: stroll
options.why: Stroll is a relaxed, pleasant walk.

options.text: march
options.why: March is quick and firm, like a soldier.

options.text: trudge
wander
options.why: Wander means to go without a plan or a direction.

hints: Think about how a tired person walks.
Look for a slow, heavy word.
Say each word in a sentence about the hiker.
items.explanation: Trudge means to walk slowly with heavy steps, which suits a tired hiker.

items.prompt: Putri finds the word luminous while reading and wants to use it in her own writing. What is the best way to record it?

options.text: Underline it in the book and move on
options.why: She may forget the meaning and not use it.

options.text: Write it in a word log with its meaning and a sentence of her own
Copy the whole page
options.why: This does not highlight the word or its meaning.

options.text: Memorise the first letter only
options.why: This will not help her use the word.

hints: A good record helps you remember and use the word.
Include the meaning and an example.
Which choice keeps the meaning and shows how to use it?
items.explanation: Recording the word, its meaning and a sentence of her own helps her use it later.

items.prompt: Choose the two synonyms for ancient.

options.text: aged
antique
brand-new
options.why: This is the opposite of ancient.

options.text: recent
options.why: This means not long ago, so it is the opposite.

hints: A synonym has a similar meaning.
Ancient means very old.
Cross out the words that mean new.
items.explanation: Aged and antique both mean old. Brand-new and recent are opposites.

items.prompt: Put these words in order from the weakest to the strongest feeling.
hints: All the words describe being glad.
Think of the size of the feeling.
Pleased is the mildest.
items.explanation: The words rise in strength: pleased, happy, delighted, overjoyed.
